books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Fort Sumter crisis as told in 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 15, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.7. Dates, hours, and casualty figures verified against the National Park Service (nps.gov/apco/april-1861.htm) and the Battle of Fort Sumter record. The facts are as stated in the books; the wording is original.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase: Fort Sumter stood on an island in Charleston Harbor, one of the last federal forts still held in the seceded South. In April 1861 President Lincoln told South Carolina he would send food, but not men or arms, to the hungry garrison. Before the supply ships arrived, Confederate guns opened fire at 4:30 in the morning on April 12. After about thirty-four hours of bombardment, Major Robert Anderson surrendered the fort on April 13. No soldier was killed by the shelling. Two days later, on April 15, Lincoln called for 75,000 militiamen to put down the rebellion, and four more slave states — Virginia, Arkansas, Tennessee, and North Carolina — left the Union.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: According to the passage, what event began the fighting of the Civil War?

options.misconception: The call for troops came after the fighting began; it was the response, not the start.

options.text: The Confederate bombardment of Fort Sumter

options.misconception: South Carolina seceded in December 1860, months before any shots were fired.
The election set the crisis in motion, but the passage dates the fighting to the bombardment of April 12.

rationales.A: The call for troops came after the fighting began; it was the response, not the start.
rationales.B: The passage says Confederate guns opened fire on April 12, and the bombardment ended with the fort's surrender — the first shots of the war.
rationales.C: South Carolina seceded in December 1860, months before any shots were fired.
rationales.D: The election set the crisis in motion, but the passage dates the fighting to the bombardment of April 12.
rationales.general:
1. The passage walks the crisis to a single morning: April 12, 4:30.
2. Guns, not speeches, open the war.
3. Background: the fort's garrison was nearly out of food, so Lincoln's resupply forced the Confederacy to choose.
4. A deadline makes a decision.
Remember: the first shots matter because they turn a political crisis into a war no one can vote away.
